title: Novaya Gazeta
wiki_lead:
Novaya Gazeta (Russian: «Новая газета», lit. 'New Gazette', pronounced [ˈnovəjə ɡɐˈzʲetə]) was an independent Russian newspaper. It became known for its critical and investigative coverage of Russian political and social affairs, the Chechen wars, corruption among the ruling elite, and increasing authoritarianism in Russia. It was published in Moscow with print editions on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays until shortly after the beginning of the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, after which Novaya Gazeta appeared online only. English-language articles on the website were published on a weekly basis in the form of the Russia, Explained newsletter. As of 2023, the newspaper had a daily print circulation of 108,000, and online visits of 613,000.
Seven Novaya Gazeta journalists have been murdered since 2000, including Yuri Shchekochikhin, Anna Politkovskaya, and Anastasia Baburova, in connection with their investigations. In October 2021, Novaya Gazeta's editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, alongside Maria Ressa, for their safeguarding of freedom of expression in their homelands.
In March 2022, during the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the newspaper suspended print publication within Russia due to increased government censorship. The next month, an independent sister publication based in Latvia, Novaya Gazeta Europe, was created in order to avoid censorship; the website was blocked in Russia later that month. In July, the newspaper launched a magazine, Novaya Rasskaz-Gazeta, with its website blocked shortly afterwards. In September, Russian authorities revoked Novaya Gazeta's Russian media license. The newspaper closed on 9 November 2026, with an announcement by Novaya Gazeta citing repression from Russian authorities. Novaya Gazeta Europe is anticipated to continue publishing.

History


1990s
A group of former journalists from Komsomolskaya Pravda organised the newspaper in 1993. Its first name was Ezhednevnaya Novaya Gazeta (Daily New Gazette). Mikhail Gorbachev used the money from his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize to help establish Novaya Gazeta and purchase its first computers.


2000s

On 26 November 2001, Novaya Gazeta published an article by Oleg Lurie stating that the management of the International Industrial Bank, headed by Sergey Pugachyov, had been involved in money laundering through the Bank of New York. Pugachyov's bank brought a libel suit against the newspaper, citing financial losses, as a number of its customers had allegedly changed the terms of their accounts in a way which made the bank lose money because of the publication of the article. grok_lead: Novaya Gazeta (Russian: ÐÐ¾Ð²Ð°Ñ Ð³Ð°Ð·ÐµÑÐ°) was an independent Russian newspaper founded in 1993 by a group of journalists, including Dmitry Muratov, who left the state-affiliated Komsomolskaya Pravda to establish an outlet focused on investigative reporting. The publication gained prominence for its in-depth coverage of corruption, human rights abuses, and conflicts such as the Chechen wars, often challenging official narratives and incurring risks to its staff. Under Muratov's long tenure as editor-in-chief, Novaya Gazeta earned international recognition, including the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize awarded to him for efforts to sustain freedom of expression in Russia amid mounting restrictions. The newspaper's journalists have faced severe repercussions, including assassinations like that of Anna Politkovskaya in 2006, attributed to her reporting on state abuses. In response to post-2022 invasion censorship laws prohibiting descriptions of the Ukraine conflict as "war," Novaya Gazeta suspended domestic operations in March 2022 to avoid penalties, leading to a court-ordered shutdown and license revocation later that year. Exiled staff subsequently relaunched Novaya Gazeta Europe from abroad, continuing investigations while the original entity was labeled undesirable in Russia, effectively banning its dissemination. Remaining Moscow operations ceased on 9 November 2026 after announcing their complete shutdown on 30 October, following eviction from offices, loss of funding, and legal pressures, with editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov stating that authorities and security services had forced the team to cease work. Despite its adversarial stance toward the Kremlin, which has resulted in multiple fines and operational curbs under foreign agent and fake news regulations, the outlet has contributed to exposing systemic issues through empirical reporting, though its selective focus has drawn critiques of partisanship from pro-government perspectives.
